summary:
We developed OUTPOST — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, a free browser game that puts children aged 7–12 in command of a Moon or Mars base. Each sol (space day) the player receives a limited power budget and must split it across five competing systems — life support, radiation shielding, food, science and crew rest. You can’t fund everything, so every choice has a real cost.

It addresses the challenge directly: children manage a lunar or Martian outpost and make genuine trade-offs about life support, shielding, power, food and communication delay. Crucially, the hazards use real NASA data, not invented numbers — solar storms come live from NASA DONKI (with an archive of real historic flares as fallback), and radiation, sol length and Earth–Mars comms delay come from NASA missions (Chang’e-4 LND, RAD/Curiosity). Each fact is labelled real vs game model in-app.

It matters because it teaches systems thinking and trade-offs, not facts to memorize — the lesson sticks because the child feels each cost. It’s free, offline-capable, bilingual, and runs on a cheap school laptop or phone.
details:
What it does and how it works

OUTPOST is a free, browser-based game that puts children aged 7–12 in command of a Moon or Mars base. The player picks a base — Moon (a 10-sol mission) or Mars (a 12-sol mission), where a sol is a space day. Each sol they are given a fixed, limited amount of power and must divide it across five competing systems: life support, radiation shielding, food, science and crew rest. You can never fund everything at once, so every decision has a cost.

Controls are deliberately simple for the age group — plus/minus steppers and one-tap “quick plans” (Balanced, Stay safe, Do science, Shield up). After the player commits a plan, the meters respond both to their choices and to that sol’s hazard: a solar flare, lunar night, a Mars dust storm, or a communications blackout. Radiation accumulates across the mission, so the player must learn to raise shielding before a flare arrives, or the crew takes a dose toward a hard limit. At the end, a Mission Report shows a sol-by-sol chart of how the base held up and lists the exact NASA datasets the simulation relied on.

Benefits and intended impact

OUTPOST teaches systems thinking and trade-offs rather than isolated facts to memorize — the lesson sticks because the child feels the cost of each choice. It is built for reach and equity: free, no download, no account, works offline as an installable Progressive Web App, so it runs on a cheap school laptop or a shared phone, including in low-connectivity regions. It is bilingual (English + Russian) with plain language and a built-in tutorial. The intended impact is scientific literacy that is honest by design: a dedicated in-app section explains what the game simplifies, so children build understanding instead of misconceptions. Our aim is a tool a teacher can hand to a seven-year-old and trust.

Real NASA data — all sources named

The hazards are not invented.

  • NASA DONKI (live) — the Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information. On mission start the game queries NASA’s live feed for recent real solar flares and turns them into in-game storms. Offline or if the call fails, it falls back to an archive of real historic flares (2003 X28, 2017 X9.3, 2024 X8.7) — never fabricated. Each flare is tagged live vs archive in-game.
  • Chang’e-4 LND — first in-situ lunar surface radiation (~1.3 mSv/day; Zhang et al., Science Advances, 2020).
  • NASA RAD / Curiosity — Mars surface radiation (~0.64 mSv/day).
  • NASA Mars facts — a sol is 24 h 39 min.
  • Lunar day/night cycle — ~29.5 Earth days.
  • Deep-space communication light-time — Earth–Mars 3–22 min; Earth–Moon ~1.3 s.

Every real fact is listed and sourced on the in-app “Real data” page, tagged REAL NASA DATA vs game model.

Tools, languages and software

Front end: React 18 + TypeScript, built with Vite, styled with Tailwind CSS. State management with Zustand; charts with Recharts. Offline/installability via vite-plugin-pwa (service worker). Live data via the NASA DONKI API. Quality: a pure game-model layer covered by 18 automated tests with Vitest. Deployed on Vercel, with security headers; the project is open-source on GitHub. No special hardware is required — it runs in any modern browser on desktop or mobile.

How it is creative

The unusual combination is this week’s real NASA space weather, inside a game a seven-year-old can play, with a transparent line drawn between real data and game model. We paired that scientific rigor with a warm, retro mission-control aesthetic — a splash intro, scroll animations and a friendly tutorial — so it feels like a game, not a lecture, while the substance underneath is real and sourced.

What our team considered

  • Age-appropriateness: three core meters to watch plus a crew-health readout and a science goal, not five or six systems at once — simple enough for a child, with quick-plan buttons so no reading is required to start.
  • Honesty: we refused to present any invented number as NASA data; everything real is sourced and everything modeled is labeled.
  • Accessibility and equity: free, offline, bilingual, installable, low-end-device friendly.
  • Validity: the model is unit-tested and the app is deployed and working; limitations (tuned resource rates, shortened missions, rounded doses) are stated openly.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (disclosure)

We used an AI assistant (Anthropic’s Claude) as a pair-programmer to help implement the React/TypeScript code, tune game balance, and assemble the demo materials. All design decisions, the selection and verification of NASA datasets, game-balance targets, and testing were directed and reviewed by the team. No AI-generated imagery is presented as real, and no fabricated numbers are presented as NASA data.
